text: Lesson 24 named ATF coverage on the critical path as a hard requirement for Course Registration, without designing it. This lesson does that design work, using the real UI Test, server-side Test, and Test Suite mechanics from Chapter 4, applied to this specific application instead of a generic example.

The critical path is one sentence: a student registers for a course. But that sentence actually covers two distinct scenarios that both have to be proven, because a student registering for an open section and a student hitting a full section exercise completely different logic. Treating the full-section case as automatically covered just because the happy path works is exactly the kind of assumption that generates support tickets, so each scenario gets its own explicit test.

Test one is a UI Test for the happy path. It opens the registration form as a logged-in student, selects a section known to have an open seat, clicks Register, then asserts the registration status reads Confirmed and that the section's open-seat count decremented by exactly one. This is the test that proves, every single time a change is proposed, that the application still does the one thing it exists to do.

Test two is a UI Test for the full-section rejection path, which the registrar's office specifically flagged as the scenario that causes problems when it's handled wrong. It selects a section seeded with zero open seats, clicks Register, and asserts three things: the status reads Rejected, Section Full, not a silent failure; the seat count did not change, because a rejected registration must never quietly consume a seat; and the student was offered the waitlist option rather than simply told no.

Test three is a server-side Test for the registration-capacity-check logic itself, independent of the UI. It calls that logic directly: with max seats thirty and enrolled count thirty, it asserts the function returns false, no seat available; with enrolled count twenty-nine, it asserts the function returns true. Testing this logic directly catches a bug in the capacity math even if a future UI change accidentally makes the broken logic look correct on screen.

All three tests get grouped into one ATF Test Suite, named Course Registration Critical Path, configured to run automatically on every pipeline build triggered by a commit to the connected repository. A regression gets caught the afternoon it's introduced, not the night before a release. That's exactly the evidence Lesson 26's deployment runbook is built around, so let's close out the capstone by writing that runbook for real.
